source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: A decade of research
finding: Rival reading of a result that looked like a failure. Richter and Spaeth (2006) reported group means that seemed to reject noncompensatory use of recognition. The authors re-ran the individual data and found most people followed recognition almost always.
numbers: Group means of recognition-consistent choices: 98% (positive cue), 95% (no cue), 82% (negative cue). Individual data, negative-cue condition: most people chose the recognized city 97-100% of 32 trials, with zero or one deviation.
limits: Authors are the theory's founders. Re-analysis of one study; individual data shown only in a figure. Others (Hilbig, Gloeckner) read similar data as compensatory.
agent_relevance: Averages can hide two groups: rule followers and non-followers. Test a simple mode per item type and per run, not only on the mean.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: A decade of research
finding: Only one study pitted compensatory models against the recognition heuristic as a prediction test. None of five compensatory models predicted better than the heuristic.
numbers: Marewski et al. (2010): five compensatory models with free parameters (able to mimic or reverse the heuristic) vs the parameter-free heuristic; heuristic best overall. Voter task with one negative cue: accordance 73%; without negative cue 87-89%.
limits: Second-hand in a review by the heuristic's authors. One study set (political candidates, cities). Only five compensatory rivals.
agent_relevance: A fair simple-vs-complex test needs rivals that predict out of sample, not only fit. Use the same rule for our mode comparisons.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: A decade of research
finding: Recognition predicted real outcomes about as well as expert rankings in some forecast tasks; accordance with the heuristic tracks recognition validity across studies.
numbers: Wimbledon 127 men's matches: recognition 72% correct; ATP Entry Ranking 66%, ATP Champions Race 68%, expert seedings 69% (Serwe & Frings 2006). Across 43 studies and domains, share of recognition-consistent judgments vs mean recognition validity r = .57.
limits: Second-hand. Serwe and Frings expected recognition to fail. Works where fame tracks success; weak where not (disease frequency, recognition valid only about 60%).
agent_relevance: A cheap familiarity signal can match experts when validity is high. Check validity per domain before trusting it.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: A decade of research
finding: Informal replications and extensions of the less-is-more effect. Evidence is mostly informal or analytic.
numbers: Goldstein (1997): about 60% of US students vs about 90% of Germans correct on a US city-size question. BBC radio replication: 65% (New York) vs 82% (London). Frosch et al. (2007): less-is-more shown for 2, 3 and 4 alternatives. Group studies: a non-recognizer's view often prevailed over majority vote.
limits: The BBC study was uncontrolled and the authors say so. Not independent replications. Group-decision proportion not extracted.
agent_relevance: Weak, mostly one-group evidence. Do not build on 'knowing less is better' without our own test.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: A decade of research
finding: Recognition use is only slightly higher when recognition leads to a right answer than when it leads to a wrong answer.
numbers: Hilbig & Pohl (2008): recognized city chosen 76% when recognition led to a wrong answer vs 82% when right. Pohl (2006): 89% adherence in city population vs 54% in a distance judgment task.
limits: Authors read the small gap as extra knowledge in use; its source is unclear and disputed (Pachur & Hertwig vs Hilbig et al.).
agent_relevance: One-reason shortcuts are softly overridden by other evidence. An S0 gate should allow override, not be a hard rule.

source: Hilbig & Richter (2011) Homo heuristicus outnumbered: Comment on Gigerenzer and Brighton (2009)
finding: Re-analysis of the data Gigerenzer and Brighton (2009) used, with a multinomial r-model separating true recognition use from guessing and knowledge. True use was lower than adherence rates suggest.
numbers: Aggregate: adherence M = .91 but estimated true use r = .80 (SE .01). Deterministic version (r=1) misfit (p<.001). Probabilistic version needed error f = .09 and still fit worse. Individual (N = 28): heuristic submodel (r=.96) fit significantly worse for 20/28 (71%). Probabilistic submodel by BIC: better for 9 (32%), tie 7 (25%), r-model better 12 (43%).
limits: Small N = 28. The authors favour compensatory views, so both sides are partisan. Results depend on r-model assumptions.
agent_relevance: High adherence is not proof of a one-reason rule. If we log mode use, we need a process check, not only outcome match.

source: Hilbig & Richter (2011) Homo heuristicus outnumbered: Comment on Gigerenzer and Brighton (2009)
finding: Model-free check: most people discriminated cases where recognition was right from cases where it was wrong, which a pure recognition rule cannot do.
numbers: Discrimination index (Hilbig & Pohl 2008): 11 of 28 (39%) within the 95% CI of zero (possible pure users); 17 of 28 (61%) reliably discriminated.
limits: A zero index also fits a person with no extra knowledge. Same small sample.
agent_relevance: Judge a one-reason mode on the cases where it is wrong, not only where it is right.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler, Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: A review of theory and tests
finding: Evidence for the less-is-more effect is mixed, and its theoretical conditions often fail in real data.
numbers: Pachur (2010) reviewed 10 data sets where recognition validity exceeded knowledge validity: effect not reliably found. Recognition and knowledge validities change with the number of recognized objects, which breaks the constant-validity assumption of Goldstein and Gigerenzer (2002). Katsikopoulos (2010): effect does not need recognition validity above knowledge validity under imperfect memory.
limits: Review; Pachur (2010) itself not opened. Effect depends on how validities change with knowledge.
agent_relevance: 'Less is more' is conditional. Treat it as a hypothesis to test on our task class.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler, Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: A review of theory and tests
finding: Recognition use varies by domain and by contradicting criterion knowledge. Where recognition is not tied to the criterion, people mostly ignore it.
numbers: Oppenheimer (2003, Exp 2): only about 30% chose the recognized object (e.g. Chernobyl vs a fictional city). Pachur & Hertwig (2006): recognition valid only about 60% for disease frequency; for leprosy vs an unrecognized disease 85% judged the unrecognized one more frequent. Lab adherence is typically about 90% when validity is high.
limits: Oppenheimer's fictional-name stimuli are criticised by the review authors. Different tasks and stimuli.
agent_relevance: Gate on the validity of the cue in the domain, not on the cue's presence.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler, Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: A review of theory and tests
finding: Individual-level data in contradicting-cue experiments show large differences. A sizeable minority always follows recognition; the rest split.
numbers: Richter & Spaeth Exp 3: 17 of 28 followed recognition with at most one exception in 32 trials; median 97% with and without contradiction; mean fell from 95% to 82%. With contradiction: 43% unchanged, 39% followed less, 18% more. Pachur et al. (2008): 23% always chose recognized despite contradicting cues. Newell & Fernandez: 48-60% zero exceptions.
limits: Percentages come from different studies and cue schemes. Review by proponents.
agent_relevance: Expect a mixture of strategies in repeated runs; report distributions across runs.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler, Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: A review of theory and tests
finding: Forecasting: laypeople's recognition predicted outcomes at or above expert-based rankings in several sports, not everywhere.
numbers: Strict recognition use gave 71% correct forecasts in one tournament study (attribution not confirmed in the text read); Snook & Cullen (2006): 85% on which NHL player had more career points; Wimbledon amateurs 73% when applicable, collective recognition 72% (replicated by Scheibehenne & Broeder 2007).
limits: Mostly sports and geography. Recognition is confounded with criterion knowledge (Oppenheimer's objection).
agent_relevance: Prominence signals in LLM outputs (entity frequency) may be strong in some domains and misleading in others.

source: Gigerenzer & Brighton (2009) Homo heuristicus: Why biased minds make better inferences
finding: Core less-is-more evidence from model comparison: tallying and take-the-best beat multiple regression out of sample across 20 data sets while using fewer cues.
numbers: Czerlinski, Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1999): 20 studies, paired comparisons, cross-validated for both tallying and regression (fixing an imbalance in Dawes and Corrigan). Take-the-best looked up 2.4 cues on average; regression and tallying 7.7. 95% CIs within +-.4 points. Ten of the 20 sets came from a regression textbook (Weisberg 1985).
limits: Small, mostly old data sets. Exact accuracies are in a figure not read. Advantage shrinks as training samples grow.
agent_relevance: Simple rules win when training data are small. Our agent has little task-specific data per item, which fits.

source: Gigerenzer & Brighton (2009) Homo heuristicus: Why biased minds make better inferences
finding: Take-the-best vs learning models: it wins under sparse data by ignoring cue dependencies.
numbers: City-population task: take-the-best beat a linear perceptron, nearest neighbour, C4.5, CART, and a conditional-validity variant across training sizes; Brighton (2006) found the same on 20 data sets. Tallying works when R squared is at most .5, objects-to-cues ratio at most 10, and cues are correlated (Einhorn & Hogarth 1975).
limits: Advantage is at small training sizes; with more data complex models catch up. Authors' own simulations.
agent_relevance: Restrict simple modes to small-sample, redundant-cue tasks.

source: Gigerenzer & Brighton (2009) Homo heuristicus: Why biased minds make better inferences
finding: Proposed rules for fair tests of heuristic use, with supporting individual-level studies.
numbers: Three rules: test models against each other; test at individual level; test adaptive selection. Bergert & Nosofsky (2007): stochastic take-the-best vs additive weighting at individual level, 'vast majority' used take-the-best. Nosofsky & Bergert (2007): most did not use an exemplar strategy.
limits: Proponents' rules. Hilbig & Richter (2011) dispute the claim that a majority use heuristics. Those tasks gave a known cue order.
agent_relevance: Use the three rules as a protocol for judging our mode selection.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making
finding: Strategy selection is learned from the environment. Take-the-best use rises where cue validities vary a lot and falls where they do not. Higher IQ went with correct strategy selection.
numbers: Rieskamp & Otto (2006): take-the-best-consistent judgments rose over trials from 28% to 71% in a high-variability environment and fell to 12% in a low-variability one. Dieckmann & Rieskamp (2007): take-the-best predicted best at high redundancy, compensatory at low. Broeder & Newell (2008): IQ relates to strategy selection, not execution.
limits: Review; originals not opened. Learning with feedback; may not transfer to one-shot judgments.
agent_relevance: Choosing the right simple mode needs feedback. Our gate should learn from outcomes.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making
finding: Applied evidence for simple rules and trees, with a flagged weakness: many comparisons were fits, not predictions.
numbers: Customer activity: hiatus heuristic 83% correct vs 75% for Pareto/NBD (airline 77% vs 74%). Child pneumonia tree 72% vs 75% for logistic regression. Michigan hospital: about 90% of chest-pain patients sent to ICU while about 25% had a heart attack. Physician prescribing: matching heuristic and regression fit equally well with less information.
limits: Review; some physician studies reported only fits, which the review itself notes. Most tree work is from the authors' network.
agent_relevance: Small trees are viable decision aids for binary calls. A candidate form for an S0 triage step.

source: Phillips, Neth, Woike, Gaissmaier (2017) FFTrees: A toolbox to create, visualize, and evaluate fast-and-frugal decision trees
finding: Out-of-sample test of fast-and-frugal trees against standard machine learning on 10 real data sets. Trees were competitive, not better.
numbers: Mean balanced accuracy, 100 simulations per model-data pair: SVM 0.86; fast-and-frugal trees 0.83; regularized logistic regression 0.83; random forest 0.83. Tree builders: fan algorithms mean 0.81 (IQR .73-.93), max 0.64, zig-zag 0.75; mean cues used 1.85 (fan) vs 4.85 (zig-zag). SVM crashed on 2 sets, so its mean covers 8.
limits: Authors built the toolbox. FFTs worst on the occupancy set. Claimed gain is transparency and speed, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: A simple tree costs a few points of accuracy for large gains in transparency and speed. Reasonable for a cheap, auditable gate.

source: Bobadilla-Suarez & Love (2018) Fast or frugal, but not both: Decision heuristics under time pressure
finding: Frugal is not fast. Take-the-best (less information) was slower and fared worse under time pressure than tallying with unordered, colour-coded cues; the pattern reversed when cues were ordered by validity and colour removed.
numbers: Two experiments with a 2000 ms deadline. Exp 1: tallying faster than take-the-best. Exp 2 (ordered cues): take-the-best faster. Exclusions in the take-the-best condition were about a quarter of participants (26% and 25% as read) vs 1% and 13% for tallying.
limits: Participants followed an instructed heuristic with cues on screen, not from memory. Speed-accuracy trade-off limits one result. Exclusion decimals partly garbled in the text.
agent_relevance: A shortcut is cheap only if cue order and format are cheap to search. Our modes need pre-sorted cue lists.

source: Castela, Kellen, Erdfelder, Hilbig (2014) The impact of subjective recognition experiences on recognition heuristic use: A multinomial processing tree approach
finding: Reanalysis of 16 published data sets: recognition-heuristic use rises when recognition comes with further knowledge, supporting a memory-state account over a pure binary-recognition rule.
numbers: 16 published data sets; MPT model estimates RH use by recognition experience (merely recognized vs recognized with knowledge). RH use was higher with further knowledge. Exact parameter values not extracted.
limits: Abstract and introduction read for this entry. Three rival accounts: pure RH, knowledge-based, memory-state heuristic.
agent_relevance: Familiarity works better with a supporting second cue. A mode with a checked second cue is safer than a bare one-cue rule.

source: Within-person adaptivity in frugal judgments from memory (2017), Psychological Research
finding: Within-person test of adaptivity: people changed reliance on recognition between a high-validity domain (city population) and a low-validity one (distance), but not in line with their own item-level validities.
numbers: N = 99. 87 of 99 changed reliance between domains. Reliance correlated across domains at 0.38 [0.15, 0.58]. Reliance vs individual recognition validity: population -0.38 [-0.74, 0.20]; distance -0.06 [-0.48, 0.39]. Confidence tracked domain, not individual validity.
limits: One online sample. Author list not confirmed in this session. Domain differences modest.
agent_relevance: People pick strategies by coarse domain feel, not by checking validity. An agent gate should compute an explicit validity signal.

source: Peltola, Jokinen, Kaski (2019) Probabilistic formulation of the Take The Best heuristic
finding: A likelihood-based take-the-best model that learns cue order and direction. On four data sets it matched or beat standard take-the-best and ABC-TTB, and beat logistic regression on three.
numbers: Four data sets (homeless, profsalary, city, mileage); 1000 train/test replications over training sizes. Better than logistic regression except on mileage, where regression is best except at the smallest training size. One MCMC iteration found good models.
limits: Four data sets. Accuracy values are in figures not read.
agent_relevance: More data erodes the simple-rule edge. Consistent with the sample-size boundary.

source: Schulz, Speekenbrink, Meder (2016) Simple trees in complex forests: Growing Take The Best by Approximate Bayesian Computation
finding: Take-the-best can be learned from smaller building blocks. The learned version recovers TTB-generated data and can beat traditional take-the-best.
numbers: Abstract-level claims: recovers TTB; sensible cue importance and direction; can outperform TTB and other models; trades performance for computation. Learning sets 5% to 90% of data in real-data tests.
limits: Proof of concept on a few data sets. Numeric results not read.
agent_relevance: Cue order and direction can be learned online, the missing piece for an adaptive gate.

source: Jagadish, Thalmann, Coda-Forno, Binz, Schulz (2026) Meta-learning ecological priors from large language models explains human learning and decision making
finding: LLM-generated task distributions plus meta-learning produced a model (ERMI) that picked the same decision strategy as people in each condition: one-reason when cues were ranked, equal weighting when direction was known, weighted when unknown.
numbers: Gini of attribute weights: ranking 0.3399 (SEM .0631, one-reason); direction 0.0743 (SEM .0138, equal weights); unknown 0.1794 (SEM .0333, weighted). Human data from Binz et al.: ERMI most frequent winner in 2-attribute (posterior model frequency 0.7299, SEM .0888) and 4-attribute (0.6284, SEM .0897) experiments. 15 experiments overall.
limits: The LLM only generates training tasks; the decision model is a small meta-learned network. Not a test of LLM reasoning itself.
agent_relevance: Ecological rationality can be learned from LLM-generated environments, so LLM priors may carry the right simple rule per environment.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free Energy Heuristics: Fast-and-frugal cognition as active inference under uncertain precision
finding: Pre-registered LLM test: on high meta-uncertainty items (non-recurrent forecasting, novel synthetic, open dilemmas, strategic uncertainty), longer chain-of-thought lowered accuracy. Paper links this to take-the-best by theory.
numbers: 7 models (Phi-3.5 3.8B, Mistral 7B, Qwen2.5 7B/14B/32B, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o), 5 CoT length conditions, 7,875 responses, 45 items (31 high-regime, 14 controls). Interaction negative at posterior probability 1.00; median high-regime drop 17.3 points (95% CrI 7.7 to 25.5); gate was more than 6 points. Definite-answer controls: no such cost.
limits: Single-author preprint, not peer reviewed. Items author-built. Effect decisive in mid-to-large models, directional in the two frontier models, absent to reversed in the two weakest. The take-the-best equivalence holds only under a stated Descending Dominance condition (theory, not tested directly).
agent_relevance: Supports capping reasoning length on uncertain items. One lead to replicate on our own tasks.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free Energy Heuristics: Fast-and-frugal cognition as active inference under uncertain precision
finding: Same paper, its own limits: scoring uses an LLM judge, the design was amended, and a pilot used one small model.
numbers: Pilot: 150 cells, Mistral-7B-Instruct via Ollama. Judge claude-sonnet-4-5 at T=0, 539 calls, 0 errors, raw agreement 91.5%. Deviations from the pre-registration logged (section 5.6).
limits: Judge agreement of 91.5% still leaves error. No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Copy the regime score (cross-prompt variance, cross-seed variance, calibration error) as a cheap uncertainty detector.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free Energy Heuristics: Fast-and-frugal cognition as active inference under uncertain precision
finding: Proposed per-item regime score for 'does more thinking hurt here'.
numbers: Combines cross-prompt variance (5 paraphrases per item), cross-seed variance and calibration error; validated by simulate-and-recover with correlation above 0.96.
limits: Validated on the authors' own simulated data, not on independent human labels.
agent_relevance: A detector our code could compute from repeated samples to route items to a short mode.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models
finding: Seven LLMs on classic cognitive-psychology tasks showed irrationality that is not human-like and is inconsistent across repeats.
numbers: Seven language models; heuristics-and-biases tasks. Abstract-level result only: wrong answers differ from human biases; large inconsistency across responses. Numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract read only. Not a test of fast-and-frugal heuristics.
agent_relevance: Cross-sample disagreement is itself a signal for routing between simple and extended modes.

source: Heuristics in judgment tasks with unrecognized elements (2019), Europe's Journal of Psychology
finding: Re-analysis of Campitelli and Labollita (2010): people who recognized no chess player still inferred nationality and Elo above chance, suggesting they used other regularities in names.
numbers: 123 participants who recognized no player.
limits: Post hoc re-analysis of one data set. Mechanism inferred, not tested. Above-chance level not extracted.
agent_relevance: 'No recognition' is not 'no information'. A fallback mode needs its own cue check.

source: Greene, Frosch, McCloy, Beaman (2014) Time to decide? Simplicity and congruity in comparative judgment
finding: Rival-theory test: response times for comparisons depended on question frame x number recognized, as magnitude-comparison theories predict.
numbers: 'Smaller' questions: shorter RTs when no options recognized. 'Larger' questions: shorter RTs when all recognized. 3-AFC (Exp 1a, 1b) and 2-AFC (Exp 2); cities and richest/poorest person.
limits: Abstract read; effect sizes not extracted. A recognition account may accommodate it if evaluation depends on the question.
agent_relevance: Question direction changes which cue feels natural. Match mode prompts to the question frame.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: Models of bounded rationality
finding: Founding simulation: a less-is-more peak appears when about half the objects are known.
numbers: German cities, recognition validity .80: with half known, 80% correct on recognition pairs and 50% on guessing pairs, about 65% overall. Take-the-best peak around 77% correct, not reached by those who knew everything. 500 simulated individuals x 6 x 84 types x 3,403 tests (about 858 million).
limits: Simulation, not human data; fixed validities. Pachur (2010) showed validities change with knowledge, so the peak is not guaranteed.
agent_relevance: The numeric base of 'less is more' is an analytic simulation under strong assumptions.
